title: dockerd memory grows until containers are OOM-killed after Docker package upgrades
body: After upgrading my dedicated servers to Docker 27.0.3, dockerd starts around 200 MB after a restart and then keeps increasing until containers can be OOM-killed. The affected Ubuntu 22.04 server runs 68 containers with the local logging driver, cgroup v2, overlay2, healthchecks, and many services managed by systemd using docker compose up without detached mode. I captured a heap profile through /debug/pprof/heap. A lightly loaded Docker 27.0.3 server that is not affected uses json-file logging and has no healthchecks. I do not yet have a minimal reproduction.

symptoms_visible: After the upgrade to Docker 27.0.3, dockerd starts near 200 MB after a restart and then keeps consuming more memory until containers can be OOM-killed.
The growth happens on my busy servers; my lightly loaded server with json-file logging and no healthchecks does not show it.
N0.label: N0 dockerd memory growth reported

symptoms_visible: dockerd memory continues growing while the containers and attached Compose services remain running.
N1.label: N1 goroutine dump collected

symptoms_visible: On my reproduction VM, Docker 27.0.3 reaches about 1 GB in roughly an hour, and stopping the containers does not release the daemon memory.
The equivalent VM stays around 350 MB with the matched Docker 26.0.0 package set, while the Docker 27.0.3 VM keeps growing.
N2.label: N2 reproducible version-dependent growth

symptoms_visible: The Docker 27.0.3 reproduction still grows in memory after I replace containerd.io with version 1.6.33.
N3.label: N3 containerd-only downgrade tested

symptoms_visible: Docker Engine 27.0.1 stays stable when I pair it with Compose 2.26.1 and Buildx 0.13.1 instead of the newer plugin packages.
On another affected host, downgrading only docker-compose-plugin to 2.26.1 keeps dockerd between about 115 and 140 MB for at least five days.
Disabling healthchecks sharply reduces the growth on affected hosts, although one host still shows a smaller amount of growth.
N4.label: N4 Compose plugin and healthcheck correlation isolated

symptoms_visible: With Compose 2.26.1, dockerd remains around 140 MB even when I start a project with COMPOSE_EXPERIMENTAL_OTEL=1.
N5.label: N5 older Compose with tracing enabled remains stable

symptoms_visible: On a Docker build containing the OpenTelemetry meter workaround, dockerd memory remains bounded while the same Compose-managed containers and healthchecks run.
N_terminal.label: terminal memory growth resolved

question_patterns: Can you capture /debug/pprof/goroutine?debug=2 from dockerd while its memory is high?
Please collect a goroutine dump using the Docker socket and attach the raw output.
clarifications.user_answer_in_this_oncall: Here you go! I ran the same curl command against /debug/pprof/goroutine?debug=2 and attached the goroutine-dump.log file.

counterfactual_candidates.answer: The dump came back tiny — just the usual idle runtime and daemon background goroutines, with no HTTP request stacks in it at all.
I captured the dump the same way, but after dockerd had reached 2 GB instead of 1 GB.

edges.comment: The reporter only handed over the raw goroutine dump the maintainer asked for. Reading that dump as full of long-running attach and events request goroutines, and interpreting those requests as unfinished OpenTelemetry work, is engineer-side analysis.

question_patterns: Can you reduce this to a reproducible environment we can inspect?
Could you reproduce the growth in a small VM and share its workload configuration?
clarifications.user_answer_in_this_oncall: I reproduced it in an Ubuntu Server 24.04 VirtualBox VM and shared the VM files and credentials. It runs nginx containers with curl healthchecks, uses the local log driver, and systemd starts docker compose up --abort-on-container-exit. dockerd reached about 1 GB in roughly an hour.

counterfactual_candidates.answer: The reduced VM stays below 400 MB indefinitely; I can only reproduce the growth on the original production servers.

question_patterns: Does stopping the containers release the accumulated dockerd memory?
What happens to daemon RSS after docker compose down?
clarifications.user_answer_in_this_oncall: Shutting down the containers does not clean up the memory already used by dockerd.

question_patterns: Can you compare the same VM workload on fully matched Docker 26.0.0 and 27.0.3 package sets?
Please test old and new Docker package sets on otherwise equivalent VMs.
clarifications.user_answer_in_this_oncall: I ran equivalent VMs for about 30 minutes. The VM with the matched Docker 26.0.0 packages stayed around 350 MB, while the Docker 27.0.3 VM kept increasing.

counterfactual_candidates.answer: Both matched package sets grow at the same rate on the equivalent VMs.
The 26.0.0 VM stays near 400 MB rather than 350 MB, while 27.0.3 still rises continuously.

question_patterns: Can you narrow the affected release range with package versions matched to each Engine release?
What happens with matched Docker 26.1.0 and 27.0.1 stacks?
clarifications.user_answer_in_this_oncall: With package versions matched to the release changelogs, Docker 26.1.0 did not grow, while Docker 27.0.1 did. I captured the memory graphs for both tests.

edges.comment: These were controlled tests on disposable cloned VMs, so they change knowledge rather than the reporter's retained production configuration.

question_patterns: Can you keep Docker 27.0.3 but downgrade containerd.io to the 1.6.33 version used by the good setup?
Please test whether replacing only containerd eliminates the growth.
clarifications.user_answer_in_this_oncall: I cloned the 27.0.3 VM and downgraded containerd.io to 1.6.33-1, the same version used by my Docker 26.0.0 VM. dockerd still leaked memory.

counterfactual_candidates.answer: With Docker 27.0.3 unchanged, downgrading only containerd.io to 1.6.33 makes dockerd stay flat for several hours.
The containerd-only downgrade slightly slows the increase, but dockerd still grows without bound.

edges.comment: This handler-requested package-version probe falsifies containerd.io as the sufficient cause. It remains a clarification-only measurement under the measurement-class rule.

question_patterns: Can you keep the 27.x Engine and test it with the older Compose and Buildx plugins?
Which individual package combination separates the growing and stable setups?
clarifications.user_answer_in_this_oncall: I installed Docker Engine 27.0.1 with docker-compose-plugin 2.26.1, docker-buildx-plugin 0.13.1, and containerd.io 1.6.33. That combination did not show the memory growth.

counterfactual_candidates.answer: Docker Engine 27.0.1 still grows with Compose 2.26.1, Buildx 0.13.1, and containerd.io 1.6.33.
The same old-plugin combination is stable with Engine 27.0.3 rather than 27.0.1.

question_patterns: Can you isolate whether downgrading only docker-compose-plugin is sufficient?
Does the daemon remain stable if you leave Engine, Buildx, and containerd unchanged and replace only Compose?
clarifications.user_answer_in_this_oncall: On my Debian 12 host, I downgraded only docker-compose-plugin to 2.26.1 and restarted Docker. dockerd then varied between 115 and 140 MB for at least five days instead of reaching about 2 GB in one day.

counterfactual_candidates.answer: Downgrading only docker-compose-plugin has no effect; dockerd still reaches about 2 GB in a day.

question_patterns: Does the growth change if the same containers run without healthchecks?
Can you compare daemon memory before and after disabling container healthchecks?
clarifications.user_answer_in_this_oncall: After I disabled the healthchecks and restarted Docker, memory stayed fairly constant on one host. On another host it still increased a little, but much more slowly and no longer caused OOMs.

edges.comment: Reports from several affected users are folded into one simulated user side. The tests isolate newer Compose as the trigger while showing that healthchecks only amplify the volume of instrumented daemon work rather than being the underlying implementation fault.

question_patterns: Can you run Compose 2.26.1 with COMPOSE_EXPERIMENTAL_OTEL=1 and report whether dockerd starts growing?
Please enable the older Compose release's experimental OpenTelemetry support for a project and monitor daemon RAM.
clarifications.user_answer_in_this_oncall: I ran docker compose down and then COMPOSE_EXPERIMENTAL_OTEL=1 docker compose up -d for one project. With Compose 2.26.1, dockerd was still stable at about 140 MB after two days.

counterfactual_candidates.answer: Compose 2.26.1 begins leaking at the same rate as the newer release as soon as I set COMPOSE_EXPERIMENTAL_OTEL=1.
The same test remains stable for three days instead of two.

edges.comment: The raw experiment shows that merely enabling tracing in Compose 2.26.1 is insufficient to reproduce the leak. Mapping the behavior to the newer OpenTelemetry dependency and its minimal reproduction is engineer inference.

solution.intent: Fix the daemon-side OpenTelemetry metrics leak that newer Compose clients expose by applying the moby/moby#48690 workaround — configuring dockerd with a no-op OpenTelemetry meter provider so the otelhttp instrumentation on the Docker API stops accumulating per-request metric instruments — then have the reporter retest a build containing the change.
solution.concrete_example: Apply the workaround from moby/moby#48690: set a no-op OpenTelemetry meter provider during dockerd startup, so the otelhttp instrumentation wrapping the Docker API no longer accumulates a metric instrument per request while the daemon has no real MeterProvider configured — the leak reproduced by the upstream minimal repro in opentelemetry-go-contrib#5190 under the OTEL version the engine vendors. Please retest a build containing the change with the same Compose services and healthchecks and monitor dockerd RSS.
solution.inference_hint: The reporter and the other affected users supplied heap and goroutine artifacts plus controlled package tests; their answers stop at what they ran and observed. Engineers read the goroutine dump as full of long-running attach and events requests, first proposed that unended spans were being retained by the BuildKit trace recorder and then walked that back (they would only be kept when the span traceID matches an ongoing build), and re-aimed at the OpenTelemetry metrics dependency that newer Compose pulls in. The mechanism finally adopted — otelhttp accumulating per-request metric instruments while no MeterProvider is configured, so nothing ever drains them — comes from the upstream minimal repro in opentelemetry-go-contrib#5190, which was confirmed to reproduce under the OTEL version the engine vendors, and the fix is the no-op meter provider added to dockerd by moby/moby#48690. None of this reasoning may be placed in a user measurement answer.

edges.comment: Technical resolution from the final maintainer analysis and moby/moby#48690. Compose 2.26.1 is a temporary mitigation and disabling healthchecks only reduces the volume of instrumented daemon work; neither replaces the daemon-side OpenTelemetry meter fix.

satisfaction_conditions: Must identify the root cause as an OpenTelemetry metrics leak inside dockerd — the otelhttp instrumentation on the Docker API accumulating metric instruments because the daemon runs with no meter provider configured — rather than a leak in the containers themselves, and must not settle on the BuildKit trace-recorder span-retention theory that was raised early in the thread and then walked back.

The diagnosis must be grounded in the heap and goroutine evidence and the controlled package matrix: matched 26.1.x is stable, 27.x can be stable with older plugins, downgrading containerd alone does not fix it, and downgrading only Compose to 2.26.1 does.

Must recommend the daemon-side workaround represented by moby/moby#48690 — installing a no-op OpenTelemetry meter provider in dockerd so the otelhttp instrumentation stops accumulating metric instruments, mirroring the upstream minimal repro in opentelemetry-go-contrib#5190 — or running a build that already contains it.

Must not present periodic daemon restarts, permanent use of an outdated Compose package, disabling healthchecks, or downgrading containerd alone as the actual fix; these are temporary mitigation, load reduction, or a falsified direction.
Must ask the reporter to verify memory remains bounded on a build containing the fix under the same Compose and healthcheck workload before declaring the issue resolved.

persona_hint.experience_level: Highly capable infrastructure operator who manages many Docker Compose services, can build controlled VMs, pin and mix Debian package versions, collect pprof artifacts, and design comparative tests, but does not claim expertise in Go or OpenTelemetry internals.
persona_hint.communication_style: Energetic, cooperative, and unusually thorough; openly labels personal theories as uncertain, posts exact commands and configurations, and iteratively narrows the problem with reproducible experiments. Multiple corroborating affected users are folded into the same simulated user side.
